Reg CC: funds availability rules for banks

MT

Mehak Tariq, CAMSNovember 25, 2026•9 min read

Reg CC, or Regulation CC, is the Federal Reserve rule that sets how quickly a bank must make deposited funds available for withdrawal and what it must tell customers about delays. It sits at 12 CFR part 229 and implements the Expedited Funds Availability Act (EFA Act) and the Check Clearing for the 21st Century Act (Check 21). For a deposit operations team, that means four jobs: apply the availability schedule, decide when an exception allows a longer hold, send the right notice on time, and keep the disclosures in line with what the bank actually does.

This guide explains public guidance and is not legal advice.

What Regulation CC covers

Under section 229.1, the Board issues the rule and issues several provisions jointly with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. Subpart B, on funds availability, is the part deposit staff use daily. Subparts C and D cover check collection and returns between banks, and substitute checks under Check 21.

The rule applies to "banks" as section 229.2(e) defines them ("banks, savings institutions, and credit unions", in the words of the 2024 final rule). The Fed's Consumer Compliance Handbook says an account "encompasses consumer and corporate accounts". A fintech that offers deposit accounts through a partner bank should confirm with that bank which availability policy and notices apply. Section 229.3 assigns enforcement by charter: the OCC, the Board, the FDIC or the NCUA.

When a deposit counts as made

Deadlines count business days after the banking day of deposit: weekdays other than the federal holidays listed in section 229.2(g). A banking day is "that part of any business day on which an office of a bank is open to the public for carrying on substantially all of its banking functions."

Section 229.19(a) sets when funds count as deposited: on receipt at a staffed facility or ATM, on the day mail arrives, and when a night depository or lock box is emptied and the deposit is available for processing. A bank may treat a deposit as made on the next banking day if it arrives on a non-banking day or after a cut-off hour the bank sets, which cannot be earlier than 2:00 p.m. (noon at ATMs, contractual branches and off-premise facilities). Funds due on a business day must be available by 9:00 a.m. local time or when teller facilities open, whichever is later.

The Reg CC funds availability schedule

The maximum times come from section 229.10 (next-day availability) and section 229.12 (the check schedule).

DepositLatest availability
Cash deposited in person to an employeeNext business day
Cash not deposited in person to an employee (other than at a nonproprietary ATM)Second business day
Electronic paymentsNext business day after the bank receives the payment
US Treasury checks deposited into the payee's accountNext business day
Postal money orders, Federal Reserve Bank and Federal Home Loan Bank checks, in-state government checks, and cashier's, certified and teller's checks, deposited into the payee's account (with any special deposit slip required)Next business day in person to an employee; otherwise second business day
On-us checks, both branches in the same state or check processing regionNext business day
The first $275 of other check deposits on a banking dayNext business day
All other checks (local checks)Second business day
Cash or checks deposited at a nonproprietary ATMFifth business day

A bank may add one business day before funds from second-day checks can be taken out in cash or by similar means, such as an electronic payment or a cashier's check, but must still make $550 available by 5:00 p.m. on the normal availability day, on top of the $275 (section 229.12(d)). Section 229.11 indexes these amounts to inflation every five years. The 2024 final rule raised them on July 1, 2025: $225 to $275, $450 to $550, and the exception threshold from $5,525 to $6,725.

The rule still mentions nonlocal checks, but the Fed's guide to Regulation CC compliance says "there are no longer any 'nonlocal' checks for purposes of Regulation CC." The Reserve Banks cut their paper check offices from 45 in 2003 to one in 2010, and "The consolidation resulted in all checks being considered 'local checks' under Regulation CC," as the agencies' 2025 RFI explains.

Exception holds and case-by-case holds

Section 229.13 lets a bank go past the schedule in six cases:

  • New accounts, during the first 30 calendar days. Checks on the special list in the table, plus traveler's checks, keep their normal availability only for the first $6,725 deposited on a banking day, with the rest due by the ninth business day. The regular check schedule does not apply. Cash and electronic payments keep their normal schedule.
  • Large deposits: check deposits over $6,725 on one banking day, for the amount above $6,725.
  • Redeposited checks, unless the check came back for a missing indorsement since added, or for a postdate that has passed.
  • Repeated overdrafts: an account negative (or that would have been, had checks been paid) on six or more banking days in the past six months, or on two or more days by $6,725 or more. The exception lasts six months after the last overdraft.
  • Reasonable cause to doubt collectibility: facts "that would cause a well-grounded belief in the mind of a reasonable person" that the check will not be paid. The belief cannot rest on the check being "of a particular class or is deposited by a particular class of persons."
  • Emergency conditions, such as an equipment failure, another bank suspending payments, or a war.

For every exception except new accounts, the bank may extend availability by a "reasonable period": up to one business day for on-us checks, five for local checks and six for nonproprietary ATM check deposits (section 229.13(h)). A bank that takes longer has to show why that was reasonable.

A bank whose disclosed policy beats the rule may also delay a particular deposit case by case, up to the regulatory limits, if its disclosure says so (section 229.16(c)). And under section 229.19(e), a hold placed on a customer's other funds because of a check cannot exceed the amount of the check.

In that June 2025 request for information on payments fraud, the OCC, the Board and the FDIC asked how holds and the reasonable cause exception work, and the Board said it "is not proposing any changes to Regulation CC at this time."

What a hold notice must say

For the large deposit, redeposit, repeated overdraft and reasonable cause exceptions, section 229.13(g) requires a written notice with five items (a one-time or per-period notice is allowed in some cases):

  1. a number or code identifying the account (it need not be more than four digits);
  2. the date of the deposit;
  3. the amount being delayed;
  4. the reason the exception was invoked;
  5. when the funds will be available.

The notice is given at the time of deposit or, if the deposit was not made in person or the facts came out later, no later than the first business day after the facts become known or the deposit is made, whichever is later. A case-by-case notice has the same first three items plus the day the funds will be available.

For reasonable cause and case-by-case holds, a bank that gives no written notice at the time of deposit cannot charge overdraft or returned check fees caused by the hold if the check is paid, unless its notice says the customer may be entitled to a refund and how to get one, and it refunds on request. For every reasonable cause hold, the bank must keep the notice "together with a brief statement of the facts giving rise to the bank's reason to doubt the collectibility of the check" (section 229.13(g)(5)).

Disclosures and posted notices

Before opening an account, the bank gives its specific availability policy disclosure (section 229.17), which must reflect the policy it follows "in most cases" and describe the exceptions it may use (section 229.16). Section 229.18 adds a notice on preprinted deposit slips, a posted notice where employees take consumer deposits, a notice at each ATM, a copy of the policy for anyone who asks, and 30 days' notice to consumer account holders before a change in availability policy. A change that speeds up availability can be disclosed up to 30 days after. The Fed's guide suggests comparing "specific instances of deposit transactions" with the disclosure and changing the practice or the disclosure when they differ.

How a deposit operations team runs Reg CC

Section 229.19(f) requires each bank to "establish procedures to ensure that the bank complies" and to give each employee a statement of the procedures for their role. Examiners using the Fed's handbook collect the availability disclosures, hold notices, special deposit slips and change-in-terms notices, and check how hold decisions are made and where records are kept. A workable procedure has seven steps:

  1. Record when the deposit was received: the channel, the banking day and whether it beat the cut-off.
  2. Classify each item against the schedule, noting whether it was deposited in person to an employee and on any special deposit slip your bank requires.
  3. Check the account for an exception: still new, over $6,725 in checks today, a redeposit, or meeting the repeated overdraft test.
  4. For a reasonable cause hold, write down the specific facts about this check. Its type, or the type of customer, is not enough.
  5. Set the release date within the reasonable period, and hold no other funds beyond the amount of the check.
  6. Send the notice with all five items on time, with fee refund language on reasonable cause and case-by-case holds.
  7. Keep the evidence for at least two years, and longer while an investigation, enforcement proceeding or lawsuit you have notice of is pending (section 229.21(g)).

Sample holds monthly against the procedure. Route complaints about held deposits through complaints triage, and check open holds in any account closure review. If your team writes this procedure down, Verkflo can run it as a versioned agent workflow that pauses for an analyst's decision and records each step in its audit log.

Civil liability

Under section 229.21, a bank that fails to comply with subpart B owes actual damages plus, in an individual action, between $125 and $1,350 as the court allows. In a class action, that additional amount is capped at the lesser of $672,950 or 1 percent of the bank's net worth. Any successful plaintiff also recovers costs and attorney's fees, and suits must be filed within one year. A bona fide error despite reasonable procedures is a defense, but "an error of legal judgment" is not.

Common questions

What is the $275 rule?

Since July 1, 2025, the first $275 of a day's check deposits (other than next-day checks) must be available on the next business day. It was $225 before.

Does the $275 apply per account or per customer?

Per customer. The rule measures it against the checks deposited on one banking day "to all accounts of the customer" (section 229.10(c)(1)(vii)).

Does Regulation CC cover business accounts?

Yes. The schedules and exceptions apply to consumer and business transaction accounts. The posted lobby notice and the 30-day change notice in section 229.18 apply to consumer accounts only.
